questions.question_text: Which of the following is true with regards to the differences between a lesion involving the left side of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and a lesion involving the right sided dorsolateral prefrontal cortex?

options.text: Left-sided lesions are associated with significant impairment in judgement.
Left-sided lesions are associated with more impaired verbal fluency.
Left-sided lesions are associated with poorer organization.
Left-sided lesions are associated with more memory impairments.
Left-sided lesions are associated with more impaired nonverbal fluency.

correct_answer.text: Left-sided lesions are associated with more impaired verbal fluency.

correct_answers.text: Left-sided lesions are associated with more impaired verbal fluency.

questions.explanation: It is important to differentiate between left-sided lesions involving the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and a right-sided lesion. Left-sided lesions are associated with more impaired verbal fluency, whereas right-sided lesions are associated with more impaired nonverbal fluency.

questions.question_text: The mesial temporal region consists of all of the following with the exception of
questions.explanation: All of the aforementioned are structures that are part of the mesial temporal region, with the exception of (e). It is important to note that left-sided lesions can lead to anterograde amnesia affecting verbal information, whereas right-sided lesions can lead to anterograde amnesia affecting nonverbal information. Bilateral lesions would lead to both verbal and nonverbal anterograde amnesia.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old male came to the outpatient clinic for his routine review. He has a lot of concerns with regards to the antipsychotics that he is on. He is keen to consider an antipsychotic that has the least amount of side effects. Which one of the following has the least number of side effects?
questions.explanation: Based on the existing literature, this is one of the medications that carries the lowest risk of QTc prolongation, lowest risk of sexual dysfunction, EPSE, dyslipidaemia, weight gain and glucose intolerance. It also carries a low risk of hyperprolactinaemia, postural hypotension and sedation.

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old female had a relapse of bipolar affective disorder and has since been started on lithium. She has recently seen her GP, who has noted that she has hypertension (BP measured was 150/90). He is keen to start her on treatment for her hypertension. Which of the following is the most suitable drug he could consider for treatment of her hypertension?

options.text: All are contraindicated; better to watch closely

questions.explanation: Furosemide would be indicated in this case. Hypertension should not be treated with thiazide or loop diuretics in a patient on lithium, since these diuretics can reduce lithium excretion and therefore cause lithium intoxication.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements regarding the inferior parietal lobule is incorrect?

options.text: It consists of both the angular gyrus and also the supramarginal gyrus.
Lesions on the right side lead to conduction aphasia.
Lesions on the left side lead to tactile agnosia.
Lesions on the right side lead to anosognosia, neglect and tactile agnosia.
Lesions on the right side lead to anosodiaphoria.

correct_answer.text: Lesions on the right side lead to conduction aphasia.

correct_answers.text: Lesions on the right side lead to conduction aphasia.

questions.explanation: It has been shown that lesions on the left side would lead to conduction aphasia, and not lesions on the right side.

questions.question_text: Patients who have been on antipsychotics for some time are likely to develop metabolic syndrome. Based on the CATIE study, which of the following antipsychotics has been proven to be greatly associated with metabolic syndrome?
questions.explanation: The key findings of the CATIE study done in 2006, which involved more than 1,500 patients with schizophrenia, are as follows: (1) the efficacy of first-generation antipsychotics was similar to that of second-generation antipsychotics; (2) olanzapine was the most effective in terms of continuation rates; (3) olanzapine is associated with greater weight gain and increases in measures of glucose and lipid metabolism.

questions.question_text: Autosomal dominant disorders result from the presence of an abnormal dominant allele, which would cause individuals to manifest the abnormal phenotype. Which of the following statements about autosomal dominant transmission is incorrect?

options.text: The phenotype is usually present in all individuals carrying the dominant allele.
The phenotype does not skip generations, and vertical transmission takes place.
If one parent is homozygous for the abnormal dominant allele, all the members will manifest the abnormal phenotype.

questions.explanation: Both males and females are affected. The phenotypic trait does not skip generations, and vertical transmission can occur. Male-to-male transmission is possible in autosomal dominant inheritance.

questions.question_text: All of the following are autosomal dominant disorders, with the exception of
questions.explanation: All of the aforementioned can be inherited in an autosomal dominant manner, with the exception of Hurler’s syndrome, which is autosomal recessive.

questions.question_text: Balint’s syndrome occurs due to a lesion involving the occipital lobe. In this syndrome, it consists of all of the following clinical signs and symptoms, with the exception of
questions.explanation: Balint’s syndrome is characterized by simultanagnosia, ocular apraxia, psychic gaze paralysis and optic ataxia. Nystagmus is not a feature of Balint’s syndrome.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about autosomal recessive disorders is correct?

options.text: Heterozygous individuals are usually carriers who do not manifest the abnormal phenotype.
The more uncommon the disorder, the more unlikely that the parents are consanguineous.
Horizontal transmission of the disorder tends to take place.
In the event that both parents carry one abnormal copy of the gene, there is a 25% chance that a child would inherit both mutations, hence expressing the disease.
When both parents are affected, all the children would be affected.

correct_answer.text: The more uncommon the disorder, the more unlikely that the parents are consanguineous.

correct_answers.text: The more uncommon the disorder, the more unlikely that the parents are consanguineous.

questions.explanation: It is actually more likely that parents of a rare autosomal recessive disorder are consanguineous. Autosomal recessive disorders require two abnormal alleles for the phenotype to be expressed.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about the methods of suicide used, based on previous epidemiological studies, is incorrect?

options.text: Psychiatric patients tend to use violent methods such as hanging, shooting and jumping from heights.
Two thirds of British men commit suicide by hanging or via vehicle exhaust fumes.
Approximately one third of British women commit suicide by jumping.
Drowning is more frequent in older people.
Jumping from height is more frequent in young people who commit suicide.

correct_answer.text: Approximately one third of British women commit suicide by jumping.

correct_answers.text: Approximately one third of British women commit suicide by jumping.

questions.explanation: All statements are correct except (c). In fact, one third of British women who die by suicide do so by hanging or using vehicle exhaust fumes, not by jumping.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about deliberate self-harm (DSH) is incorrect?

options.text: Within the United Kingdom, the rate of DSH is rising among Asian women.
The Goth subculture in the UK is not strongly associated with self-harm.
Adverse life events tend to have occurred just prior to the act of self-harm.
A known history of DSH is a long-term predictor of suicide; risk is 100 times greater than the general population.
Fifteen percent of people who have attempted self-harm are likely to attempt another episode within the next year.

correct_answer.text: The Goth subculture in the UK is not strongly associated with self-harm.

correct_answers.text: The Goth subculture in the UK is not strongly associated with self-harm.

questions.explanation: The Goth subculture in the UK has been shown to be strongly associated with self-harm. All other statements are correct.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about the hippocampus is incorrect?

options.text: It lies mainly in the floor of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle.
Anteriorly, it forms the pes hippocampus.
Posteriorly, it ends inferior to the splenium of the corpus callosum.
It is histologically made up of four different layers.
Axons from each alveus converge medially to form the fimbria and the crus of the fornix.

correct_answer.text: It is histologically made up of four different layers.

correct_answers.text: It is histologically made up of four different layers.

questions.explanation: Histologically, the hippocampus is made up of three layers: the molecular layer, the pyramidal cell layer and the polymorphic layer.

questions.question_text: All of the following statements about X-linked recessive inheritance are correct, with the exception of which of the following?

options.text: Male-to-male transmission usually does not take place.
A heterozygote carrier woman would pass the allele to half of her sons (affected) and half of her daughters (unaffected).
Males are more likely to be affected with X-linked recessive disorders.
Females are equally likely to be affected with X-linked recessive disorders.

correct_answer.text: Females are equally likely to be affected with X-linked recessive disorders.

correct_answers.text: Females are equally likely to be affected with X-linked recessive disorders.

questions.explanation: Females are much less likely to be affected than males; they are usually carriers with minimal or no manifestation of the disorder.

questions.question_text: The age of onset of bipolar disorder has been known to be much earlier than for that of unipolar disorder. What is the average mean age of onset?
questions.explanation: The mean age of onset of bipolar disorder has been estimated to be around 30 years (range 15–50).

questions.question_text: Which of the following syndromes does not involve chromosomal deletion?
questions.explanation: Fragile X syndrome is an X-linked dominant disorder caused by CGG repeat expansion, not by a chromosomal deletion.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not considered an autosomal recessive disorder?
questions.explanation: Fragile X syndrome is X-linked dominant, not autosomal recessive.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about the epidemiology of bipolar disorder is incorrect?

options.text: Women are as likely to have the disorder as men.
Rapid cycling is much more common in women than in men.
The first onset is usually that of a manic episode.
Bipolar disorder is found in occupations requiring marked creativity.
Genetic factors play a significant role in transmission.

correct_answer.text: The first onset is usually that of a manic episode.

correct_answers.text: The first onset is usually that of a manic episode.

questions.explanation: The first onset of bipolar disorder is more commonly a depressive episode rather than a manic episode.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old woman has come to consult you for management of her insomnia. She has never managed to sleep before 3 am since adolescence and now must wake at 6 am. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Sleep disorder related to chaotic lifestyle

questions.explanation: Delayed sleep phase syndrome is characterized by normal sleep architecture and duration but a late sleep onset (around 3 am) and difficulty rising early. Treatment includes strict sleep–wake schedules, light therapy and melatonin.

questions.question_text: The Papez circuit was a concept introduced in 1937 to describe a neuronal mechanism of emotions. All of the following are part of this circuit, with the exception of
questions.explanation: The Papez circuit consists of the hippocampus, hypothalamus, anterior thalamic nucleus and cingulate gyrus. The posterior thalamic nucleus is not part of the circuit.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is considered the largest of all the cranial nerves?
questions.explanation: The trigeminal nerve is the largest cranial nerve and has four nuclei (main sensory, spinal sensory, mesencephalic and motor).

questions.question_text: Which of the following clinical signs and symptoms is not observed in neuroleptic malignant syndrome?

options.text: Rapidly varying and fluctuating changes in blood pressure

questions.explanation: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome presents with hyperthermia, rigidity, autonomic instability (fluctuating BP), elevated CK and leukocytosis. Myoclonus is not a typical feature.

questions.question_text: Which terminology describes the concept that a disorder occurs at earlier ages or with greater severity in succeeding generations?
questions.explanation: Anticipation refers to the phenomenon in autosomal dominant disorders (e.g. Huntington’s disease) where disease onset becomes earlier or more severe in successive generations.

questions.question_text: Age-specific mortality rate is correctly described as

options.text: The number of deaths over the mid-year population in one year
The number of deaths of a specific age over the mid-year population of that age in one year
Mortality due to a condition over the population with the condition in a time period
The number of deaths over the mid-year population over ten years
The number of deaths of a specific age over the mid-year population of that age over five years

correct_answer.text: The number of deaths of a specific age over the mid-year population of that age in one year

correct_answers.text: The number of deaths of a specific age over the mid-year population of that age in one year

questions.explanation: Age-specific mortality rate is the number of deaths at a specific age divided by the mid-year population of that age in one year.

questions.question_text: A 65-year-old man had a stroke four months ago and now has low mood, irritability, poor sleep and anhedonia. Post-stroke depression is most likely associated with a lesion in which part of the brain?
questions.explanation: Post-stroke depression is most commonly associated with lesions in the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (front) and left caudate nucleus.

questions.question_text: This term refers to inheriting both homologues of a chromosome pair from the same parent. Which is correct?
questions.explanation: Uniparental disomy occurs when both copies of a chromosome pair are inherited from the same parent.

questions.question_text: Apart from macroscopic changes in Alzheimer’s disease, which histopathological finding is absent?
questions.explanation: Lewy plaques are not a feature of Alzheimer’s disease. The other changes (neuronal loss, astrocytosis, neurofibrillary tangles and neuritic plaques) are characteristic.

questions.question_text: Which statement regarding Pick’s disease is incorrect?

options.text: Selective asymmetrical atrophy of anterior temporal lobes is noted.
Pick’s bodies, neuronal loss and reactive astrocytosis are present.
Changes affect cerebral cortex, basal ganglia, locus coeruleus and substantia nigra.

questions.explanation: Sulcal widening is characteristic of Alzheimer’s dementia, not Pick’s disease.

questions.question_text: A 60-year-old male discontinues SSRI due to sexual side-effects. Which adjunct may help?
questions.explanation: Bupropion, with noradrenergic activity and minimal serotonergic action, has the least impact on sexual function.

questions.question_text: The main assumptions underlying twin studies exclude which of the following?

options.text: Both monozygotic and dizygotic twins share the same environment equally.
Risk of the disorder is the same for monozygotic and dizygotic twins (null hypothesis).
Risk of the disorder is the same in twins and singletons (null hypothesis).
Risk of the disorder is increased when environmental and genetic risk factors interact.

correct_answer.text: Risk of the disorder is increased when environmental and genetic risk factors interact.

correct_answers.text: Risk of the disorder is increased when environmental and genetic risk factors interact.

questions.explanation: Twin studies assume (C) and (D) as the null hypotheses. (E) describes gene–environment interaction and is not a null assumption.

questions.question_text: Roughly what percentage of people who have committed suicide saw their GP in the week before ending their life?
questions.explanation: Approximately 40% of people who committed suicide had seen their GP in the week before their death.

questions.question_text: As compared to Parkinson’s disease, higher densities of Lewy bodies have been found in which region, with the exception of
questions.explanation: Lewy body density is higher in cingulate gyrus, parahippocampal gyrus, temporal cortex and parietal cortex but not in the basal ganglia.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not one of the usual difficulties associated with adoption studies when applied to psychiatric disorders?

options.text: Few cases fulfill adoption study criteria.
Adoption studies take a long time.
Information about the biological father may be unavailable.
Adoption might cause indeterminate psychological sequelae for adoptees.
The process of adoption can be randomized.

correct_answer.text: The process of adoption can be randomized.

correct_answers.text: The process of adoption can be randomized.

questions.explanation: Randomization is not possible in the adoption process, making (e) incorrect and highlighting a core difficulty in adoption research.

questions.question_text: The mean age of onset of obsessive-compulsive disorder has been estimated to be around
questions.explanation: The mean age of onset of OCD is around 20 years, with 70% having onset before age 25.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about the epidemiology of OCD is incorrect?

options.text: Females are more affected than males (ratio 1.5:1).
In men, checking rituals and ruminations are more common.
In women, obsessional doubts are more common.
About 50% of OCD patients are unmarried.
OCD is associated with PANDAS and post-encephalitis.

correct_answer.text: In women, obsessional doubts are more common.

correct_answers.text: In women, obsessional doubts are more common.

questions.explanation: In women with OCD, compulsive washing and avoidance are more common. Checking and ruminations predominate in men.

questions.question_text: A foundation year trainee intends to refer a person with anxiety disorder to a hypnotherapist. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Hypnosis is recommended by NICE for anxiety disorders or PTSD.
Hypnosis is superior to relaxation exercises.
Suggestion under hypnosis is superior to suggestion without hypnosis.
Sudden removal of symptoms by suggestion under hypnosis can lead to rebound depression and anxiety.
Hypnosis can aid recall in psychotherapy, leading to a better outcome.

correct_answer.text: Sudden removal of symptoms by suggestion under hypnosis can lead to rebound depression and anxiety.

correct_answers.text: Sudden removal of symptoms by suggestion under hypnosis can lead to rebound depression and anxiety.

questions.explanation: Sudden removal of symptoms by suggestion under hypnosis may lead to rebound depression and anxiety. Hypnosis is not routinely recommended by NICE for anxiety disorders.

questions.question_text: Which statement about Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (CJD) is incorrect?

options.text: CJD is transmitted via infection with a prion.
Degeneration occurs in spinal cord long descending tracts.
It usually has a relatively short incubation period.
Infection may be transmitted from surgical specimens, post-mortem preparation and human pituitary glands.
A new variant of CJD has been reported.

correct_answer.text: It usually has a relatively short incubation period.

correct_answers.text: It usually has a relatively short incubation period.

questions.explanation: CJD has a long incubation period, often years. The other statements about prion transmission and pathology are correct.

questions.question_text: A 35-year-old man presented with dyscalculia, left-right disorientation and digital agnosia. Which area of his brain is affected?
questions.explanation:
The man suffered from Gerstmann’s syndrome, which affects the 
dominant parietal lobe. Individuals present with the following:
• Dyscalculia
• Finger agnosia
• Left-right disorientation
• Agraphia

questions.question_text: A 49-year-old woman presents with persistent severe distressing pain despite negative investigations. What is the lifetime prevalence rate of this disorder?
questions.explanation: The lifetime prevalence of somatoform pain disorder is approximately 12.3%.

questions.question_text: Which of the following mutations would not result in any alteration in the amino acid residue encoded?
questions.explanation: A silent mutation changes the DNA sequence without altering the encoded amino acid.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is false?

options.text: The DRD3 Ser9Gly polymorphism is correlated with tardive dyskinesia.
The HLA gene is implicated in clozapine-induced agranulocytosis.
The serotonin transporter polymorphism is associated with antidepressant response.
The serotonin transporter gene is implicated in methylphenidate response in ADHD.
The 5-HT₂A gene is implicated in response to electroconvulsive therapy.

correct_answer.text: The serotonin transporter gene is implicated in methylphenidate response in ADHD.

correct_answers.text: The serotonin transporter gene is implicated in methylphenidate response in ADHD.

questions.explanation: In ADHD, it is the dopamine transporter gene (DAT1), not the serotonin transporter gene, that influences response to methylphenidate.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is false?

options.text: Phenytoin, valproate and clomipramine are 90%–95% protein bound.
Amitriptyline, imipramine, chlorpromazine and diazepam are 95%–99% protein bound.
If a drug is highly protein bound, its volume of distribution is reduced and close to plasma volume.
Ionized drugs cross the blood–brain barrier rapidly.
The therapeutic window is the range of plasma concentrations that yields therapeutic success.

correct_answer.text: Ionized drugs cross the blood–brain barrier rapidly.

correct_answers.text: Ionized drugs cross the blood–brain barrier rapidly.

questions.explanation: Ionized drugs (highly basic or acidic) cross the blood–brain barrier slowly, not rapidly.

questions.question_text: Which statement about loss-of-function mutations is incorrect?

options.text: They result in reduced activity or quantity of the gene product.
Mode of inheritance is usually autosomal.
Mode of inheritance can also be X-linked.
Heterozygotes often have sufficient 50% enzyme activity for normal function.
Huntington’s disease is a result of a loss-of-function mutation.

correct_answer.text: Huntington’s disease is a result of a loss-of-function mutation.

correct_answers.text: Huntington’s disease is a result of a loss-of-function mutation.

questions.explanation: Huntington’s disease results from a gain-of-function mutation (expanded CAG repeats), not a loss-of-function mutation.

questions.question_text: Which statement regarding the pharmacokinetics of psychotropic drugs is false?

options.text: Psychotropic drugs are absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract as they are lipophilic.
They must reach the CNS in adequate amounts to produce therapeutic effects.
They are mainly metabolized by the liver.
They are mainly excreted by the liver.
They are not highly ionized at physiological pH levels.

correct_answer.text: They are mainly excreted by the liver.

correct_answers.text: They are mainly excreted by the liver.

questions.explanation: Psychotropic drugs are primarily excreted by the kidneys, not the liver.

questions.question_text: The pharmacodynamic action of agomelatine involves
questions.explanation: Agomelatine is a melatonergic agonist at MT₁ and MT₂ receptors and a 5-HT₂C antagonist.

questions.question_text: Neuroanatomical areas demonstrating significant changes before and after antipsychotic treatment in first-episode schizophrenia include all, except
questions.explanation: The postcentral gyrus (somatosensory cortex) shows the least change after antipsychotic treatment, whereas the amygdala, cerebellum, frontal eye fields and prefrontal cortex do show significant changes.

questions.question_text: Which feature is not seen in punch-drunk syndrome (post-traumatic dementia)?

options.text: Perforation of the cavum septum pellucidum

questions.explanation: Punch-drunk syndrome shows cerebral atrophy, ventricular enlargement (not shrinkage), perforation of the cavum septum pellucidum, thinning of the corpus callosum, neuronal loss and neurofibrillary tangles.

questions.question_text: An 18-year-old woman with borderline personality disorder, BMI 30 kg/m², seeks a mood stabilizer that causes weight loss. Which of the following is most likely to cause weight loss?
questions.explanation: Topiramate is the mood stabilizer among these options most associated with weight loss.

questions.question_text: Which statement about the epidemiology of dementia is incorrect?

options.text: There is an equal male-to-female ratio.
Risk increases with age: 2% at 65–70 years, 20% at ≥ 80 years.
Risk factors include smoking, sedentary lifestyle, high-fat/salt diet and head injury.
Level of educational attainment does not play a role.

correct_answer.text: Level of educational attainment does not play a role.

correct_answers.text: Level of educational attainment does not play a role.

questions.explanation: Educational attainment is a recognized protective factor against dementia; low education is associated with higher risk.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is considered to be a neuropeptide transmitter?
questions.explanation: Somatostatin is a neuropeptide transmitter with largely inhibitory actions; its CSF levels are decreased in depression and Alzheimer’s disease.

questions.question_text: Antidepressants and antipsychotics might cause dizziness in a minority of patients. This might be attributed to the blockage of which of the following receptors?
questions.explanation: Some TCAs and antipsychotics cause sedation and postural hypotension via blockade of α-1 adrenergic receptors.

questions.question_text: Down’s syndrome is a result of a mutation on which of the following?
questions.explanation: An extra copy of the amyloid precursor protein gene on chromosome 21 causes Down’s syndrome.

questions.question_text: Vasoactive intestinal peptide helps to stimulate release of ACTH, GH and prolactin. It is found in all of the following structures, with the exception of which?
questions.explanation: VIP is present in cortex, hypothalamus, amygdala and hippocampus but not in the cerebellum.

questions.question_text: It has been estimated that roughly what percentage of patients with late paraphrenia have symptoms resembling paranoid schizophrenia?
questions.explanation: Approximately 60% of late-paraphrenia patients display paranoid-schizophrenia–like symptoms.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about Huntington’s disease is incorrect?

options.text: It results from a mutation of the protein huntingtin.
Characterized by selective loss of discrete neuronal populations and progressive neostriatal atrophy.
Marked atrophy of the corpus striatum is noted.
Marked atrophy of the cerebral cortex is noted.
There is a reduction in size of the lateral and the third ventricles.

correct_answer.text: There is a reduction in size of the lateral and the third ventricles.

correct_answers.text: There is a reduction in size of the lateral and the third ventricles.

questions.explanation: In Huntington’s disease, the lateral and third ventricles are enlarged, not reduced.

questions.question_text: Mutation in the following genes would result in schizophrenia, with the exception of
questions.explanation: DISC-1, DISC-2, 6p and COMT have been linked to schizophrenia; 11p is associated with BDNF and bipolar disorder.

questions.question_text: Usage of SSRIs such as fluoxetine on a long-term basis has been known to cause some sexual dysfunction. This is mainly due to action on which receptors?
questions.explanation: Agonism at 5-HT2A receptors is linked to SSRI-induced sexual dysfunction.

questions.question_text: Which antipsychotic has been linked to relatively high incidences of significant agranulocytosis?
questions.explanation: Clozapine carries the highest risk of agranulocytosis, especially in certain populations.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most common type of cerebral tumour?
questions.explanation: Gliomas (astrocytomas, oligodendrogliomas, ependymomas) are the most frequent cerebral tumours.

questions.question_text: Older antipsychotics often cause tardive dyskinesia. Which statement best explains this side effect?

options.text: Due to high D₂ receptor occupancy.

questions.explanation: Tardive dyskinesia arises from dopamine D₂ receptor supersensitivity after chronic blockade.

questions.question_text: The gene responsible for dementia development in Down’s syndrome patients is
questions.explanation: Trisomy 21 leads to overexpression of the APP gene, predisposing to early-onset Alzheimer’s.

questions.question_text: Which of the following changes is implicated in the neuropathology of OCD?
questions.explanation: Hyperactivity of the orbitofrontal cortex is a key finding in OCD neuroimaging.

questions.question_text: During which phase of mitosis does the cell replicate its genetic material prior to further division?
questions.explanation: DNA replication occurs during interphase before the mitotic divisions.

questions.question_text: In idiopathic Parkinson’s disease, Lewy bodies are present in all of the following structures, with the exception of
questions.explanation: Lewy bodies occur in SN, hypothalamus, cortex and olfactory bulb but not in the hippocampus.

questions.question_text: What is the estimated prevalence of dementia at age 80?
questions.explanation: Dementia prevalence at age 80 is approximately 20%.

questions.question_text: A 20-year-old male with post–head injury seizures is to start an anti-epileptic. Which has the least cognitive impact?
questions.explanation: Lamotrigine has a lower risk of cognitive side effects compared to older anticonvulsants.

questions.question_text: Which statement about switching antidepressants is incorrect?

options.text: When switching, consider another SSRI or well-tolerated new-generation agent.
Switch over 2 weeks for drugs with a short half-life.
A 2-week washout is essential when switching from fluoxetine to others or from paroxetine to TCAs.
A 2-week washout is also required when switching to or from MAOIs.
Drugs with shorter half-lives usually require shorter switch-over periods.

correct_answer.text: Switch over 2 weeks for drugs with a short half-life.

correct_answers.text: Switch over 2 weeks for drugs with a short half-life.

questions.explanation: Short half-life drugs usually need only about 1 week for a safe switch, not 2 weeks.

questions.question_text: Which statement regarding neurochemical changes in Alzheimer’s disease is incorrect?

options.text: There is a reduction in acetylcholinesterase.
There is a reduction in choline acetyltransferase.
There is an increase in GABA.
There is a decrease in GABA.
There is a decrease in noradrenaline.

correct_answer.text: There is an increase in GABA.

correct_answers.text: There is an increase in GABA.

questions.explanation: GABA levels are decreased in Alzheimer’s disease, not increased.

questions.question_text: Which term refers to the number of deaths under 1 year old compared to live births in one year?
questions.explanation: Infant mortality rate = deaths under 1 year ÷ live births per year.

questions.question_text: Which statement about brain changes in schizophrenia is incorrect?

options.text: Significant reduction in brain mass versus controls.
Reduction in volumes of hemispheres, cortex and central grey matter.
White matter volume is reduced in patients.
Ventricular enlargement particularly affects the temporal horn.
Temporal horn enlargement indicates temporal lobe pathology.

correct_answer.text: White matter volume is reduced in patients.

correct_answers.text: White matter volume is reduced in patients.

questions.explanation: Studies show white matter volume is not significantly reduced in schizophrenia.

questions.question_text: Neuroimaging and pathology studies show hypoplasia of which in autism?
questions.explanation: Hypoplasia of the cerebellar vermis is a consistent finding in autism.

questions.question_text: Deaths in the first 28 days divided by live births over a year is called:
questions.explanation: Neonatal mortality rate = deaths in first 28 days ÷ live births per year.

questions.question_text: A man with social phobia is repeatedly exposed to crowds. This technique is based on which principle?
questions.explanation: Repeated exposure leads to extinction of the conditioned fear response.

questions.question_text: Which statement about meiosis is incorrect?

options.text: It involves two stages of cell division.
Chromosomal division takes place once and gametes are haploid.
There is an interphase before the second division.
Prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase occur in both divisions.

correct_answer.text: There is an interphase before the second division.

correct_answers.text: There is an interphase before the second division.

questions.explanation: There is no interphase before the second meiotic division.

questions.question_text: Which is not a cognitive error usually targeted in CBT?
questions.explanation: Trial interpretation is a concept in CAT, not a standard cognitive distortion in CBT.

questions.question_text: A study reports number of stillbirths and neonatal deaths in a year. Which mortality index should be used?
questions.explanation: Perinatal mortality rate includes stillbirths and deaths <7 days among live births and stillbirths.

questions.question_text: Which statement about clinical application of CBT is incorrect?

options.text: CBT is helpful for mild depression.
CBT is of use for addictions such as alcohol.
Homework tasks are assigned between sessions.
CBT focuses on both cognitive and behavioural aspects.
CBT focuses on changing maladaptive procedural sequences.

correct_answer.text: CBT focuses on changing maladaptive procedural sequences.

correct_answers.text: CBT focuses on changing maladaptive procedural sequences.

questions.explanation: Changing procedural sequences is a focus of CAT, not standard CBT.

questions.question_text: This statistic expresses the benefit of active treatment over placebo:
questions.explanation: Number needed to treat (NNT) quantifies how many patients must be treated for one to benefit compared to placebo.

questions.question_text: ‘Morbid risk’ is the lifetime incidence in relatives. What is the morbid risk of schizophrenia among first-degree relatives?
questions.explanation: First-degree relatives have about a 3.5% lifetime risk of schizophrenia.

questions.question_text: In CBT supervision for OCD, what is the first recommended step?

options.text: Taking a detailed history of current symptoms
Using basic behavioural techniques like relaxation

correct_answer.text: Taking a detailed history of current symptoms

correct_answers.text: Taking a detailed history of current symptoms

questions.explanation: The initial phase involves detailed history-taking and psychoeducation before targeting distortions or exposures.

questions.question_text: Strategic family therapy for expressed emotion commonly uses which technique?
questions.explanation: Paradoxical interventions (prescribing or paradoxically intensifying symptoms) are a hallmark of strategic family therapy.

questions.question_text: What is the estimated morbid risk of depressive disorder among first-degree relatives?
questions.explanation: The lifetime risk of depression among first-degree relatives is about 9%.

questions.question_text: Which antipsychotic usually has the lowest risk of inducing sedation?
questions.explanation: Aripiprazole is among the least sedating antipsychotics.

questions.question_text: Which psychiatric disorder is contraindicated for brief dynamic psychotherapy?
questions.explanation: Active substance abuse is a contraindication for brief dynamic psychotherapy.

questions.question_text: What is the average age of onset of bipolar disorder among first-degree relatives?
questions.explanation: Epidemiological studies estimate the mean onset age in first-degree relatives at 21.

questions.question_text: In Kohlberg’s conventional stage of morality, which is true?

options.text: Involves obeying what authority deems appropriate.
Involves weighing individual benefits against risks.

correct_answer.text: Involves obeying what authority deems appropriate.

correct_answers.text: Involves obeying what authority deems appropriate.

questions.explanation: Conventional morality emphasizes obeying rules and authority to gain approval and avoid censure.

questions.question_text: Which is not part of the Big Five personality traits?
questions.explanation:
Based on Eysenck’s theory, the following are part of what he has 
proposed: neuroticism/stability, extroversion/introversion, psychoticism/stability 
and intelligence.

questions.question_text: What is the estimated morbid risk of Alzheimer’s disease among first-degree relatives compared to the general population?
questions.explanation: First-degree relatives have a 15%–19% lifetime risk, about three times that of the general population.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a psychodynamic psychotherapy technique?
questions.explanation: Homework assignments are typical in CBT, not core to psychodynamic therapy.

questions.question_text: Client factors making one unsuitable for brief dynamic psychotherapy include

options.text: Strong motivation to understand past influences
Capacity to form but not sustain relationships

correct_answer.text: Capacity to form but not sustain relationships

correct_answers.text: Capacity to form but not sustain relationships

questions.explanation: An inability to sustain relationships contraindicates brief dynamic psychotherapy.

questions.question_text: What is the estimated concordance rate for schizophrenia in monozygotic twins?
questions.explanation: Monozygotic twin concordance for schizophrenia is about 46%.

questions.question_text: A patient on an SSRI complains of sleep disturbance. Stimulation of which receptor is implicated?
questions.explanation: Stimulation of 5-HT2A receptors is associated with SSRI-induced insomnia.

questions.question_text: A soccer player misses a goal and concludes he will fail in all areas of life. Which cognitive distortion is this?
questions.explanation: Overgeneralization involves applying a specific failure to all aspects of life.

questions.question_text: What is the estimated concordance rate for bipolar disorder in monozygotic twins?
questions.explanation: Monozygotic twin concordance for bipolar disorder is about 40%.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a type of adoption study?
questions.explanation: Adoption studies typically involve adoptee, adoptee-family, cross-fostering and MZ twin designs; DZ twin designs are not used.

questions.question_text: In cognitive analytic therapy, the therapist focuses on which of the following?
questions.explanation: CAT emphasizes reciprocal role procedures and maladaptive procedural sequences.

questions.question_text: Which technique is not commonly used in CBT?
questions.explanation: Identifying dilemmas and snags is specific to CAT, not standard CBT.

questions.question_text: What is the estimated concordance for alcohol dependence in monozygotic twins?
questions.explanation: Concordance for alcohol dependence in MZ twins is approximately 60%.

questions.question_text: A man admitted after para-suicide and alcohol misuse needs detox. Which medication is most helpful?
questions.explanation: Oxazepam, a short-acting benzodiazepine, is preferred in suspected liver impairment.

questions.question_text: Which adoption study compares adopted children of affected and unaffected biological parents?
questions.explanation: Adoptee studies compare outcomes in adoptees with affected versus unaffected biological parents.

questions.question_text: Individuals with narcissistic personality disorder commonly use which defence mechanism?
questions.explanation: Narcissistic individuals often employ projective identification to attribute unwanted aspects of the self to others.

questions.question_text: Which intrauterine infection is least likely to result in learning disabilities?
questions.explanation: Congenital CMV, rubella, toxoplasmosis and syphilis can cause cognitive impairment; influenza B does not.

questions.question_text: The five core factors in the Big Five theory include all except:
questions.explanation: The Big Five are extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, neuroticism and openness.

questions.question_text: Which personality disorder causes the most occupational impairment?
questions.explanation: Borderline PD leads to severe occupational and interpersonal dysfunction and higher suicide risk.

questions.question_text: Which statement about the epidemiology of schizophrenia is incorrect?

options.text: Age of onset is between 25 and 45 years.
Onset is earlier in men than women.
More common in lower social classes.

correct_answer.text: Age of onset is between 25 and 45 years.

correct_answers.text: Age of onset is between 25 and 45 years.

questions.explanation: Onset typically occurs between ages 15 and 45, not only 25–45.

questions.question_text: Which index represents deaths in the first 28 days compared to live births?
questions.explanation: Neonatal mortality rate = deaths in first 28 days ÷ live births.

questions.question_text: The average 1-year incidence rate for social phobia in the general population is estimated at
questions.explanation: One-year prevalence of social phobia is about 6% in the general population.

questions.question_text: Which index represents stillbirths and deaths <7 days old compared to live births and stillbirths?
questions.explanation: Perinatal mortality rate includes stillbirths and early neonatal deaths (<7 days) per total births.

questions.question_text: The average 1-year incidence rate for panic disorder in the general population is estimated at
questions.explanation: One-year prevalence of panic disorder is approximately 10%.

questions.question_text: In MAOI-induced hypertensive crisis from tyramine (e.g., cheese), which is the emergency treatment?
questions.explanation: Phentolamine, a nonselective α-adrenergic antagonist, is indicated for MAOI-induced hypertensive crises.

questions.question_text: Huntington’s disease

options.text: Loss of dopaminergic neurons in substantia nigra
Selective loss of discrete neuronal population

correct_answer.text: Selective loss of discrete neuronal population

correct_answers.text: Selective loss of discrete neuronal population

questions.explanation: Huntington’s disease is characterized by progressive degeneration and atrophy of the neostriatum.

questions.question_text: Parkinson disease

options.text: Loss of dopaminergic neurons in substantia nigra
Selective loss of discrete neuronal population

correct_answer.text: Loss of dopaminergic neurons in substantia nigra

correct_answers.text: Loss of dopaminergic neurons in substantia nigra

questions.explanation: Idiopathic Parkinson’s disease features loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra.

questions.question_text: Autism

options.text: Loss of dopaminergic neurons in substantia nigra
Selective loss of discrete neuronal population

questions.explanation: Autism is associated with hypoplasia of the cerebellar vermis on neuropathology and imaging.

questions.question_text: Schizophrenia

options.text: Loss of dopaminergic neurons in substantia nigra
Selective loss of discrete neuronal population

questions.explanation: Schizophrenia commonly shows enlargement of the temporal horn of the lateral ventricle.

questions.question_text: This occurs in the postsynaptic membrane due to the release of an excitatory neurotransmitter.
questions.explanation: Excitatory postsynaptic potentials (EPSPs) are produced by excitatory neurotransmitters at synapses.

questions.question_text: This occurs in the postsynaptic membrane due to the release of an inhibitory neurotransmitter.
questions.explanation: Inhibitory postsynaptic potentials (IPSPs) are produced by inhibitory neurotransmitters at synapses.

questions.question_text: It is noted that one excitatory postsynaptic potential might not be enough to give rise to an action potential.
questions.explanation: Summation (temporal or spatial) is required when a single EPSP is insufficient to reach threshold.

questions.question_text: This refers to the period in which the initiation of conduction of another action potential is not possible.
questions.explanation: The absolute refractory period is the time during which no new action potential can be initiated.

questions.question_text: This refers to the period in which the initiation of conduction of another action potential is more difficult.
questions.explanation: The relative refractory period follows the absolute refractory period, requiring stronger stimuli to elicit an action potential.

questions.question_text: This form of depression has clinical features of motor retardation or agitation, anorexia, excessive guilt, diurnal variation, absence of mood reactivity and terminal insomnia.
questions.explanation: Endogenous depression is characterized by biological symptoms, diurnal variation and lack of reactivity.

questions.question_text: This commonly refers to the presence of an additional mood component on top of a background of chronically low mood.
questions.explanation: Double depression describes major depressive episodes superimposed on dysthymia.

questions.question_text: In this form of depression, after recovery the patient can recall events during illness, and patients are unresponsive when unwell.
questions.explanation: Depressive stupor presents with psychomotor suppression; patients later recall events exactly.

questions.question_text: The presence of one or two episodes of mood symptoms per month is characteristic of which condition?
questions.explanation: Recurrent brief depression involves frequent, brief (less than 2 weeks) depressive episodes.

questions.question_text: In this form of depression, depressed mood is not always complained of; instead somatic symptoms predominate.
questions.explanation: Masked depression features somatic complaints rather than overt low mood.

questions.question_text: The main function of which peptide hormone appears to be pigmentation?
questions.explanation: Melanocyte-stimulating hormone primarily regulates skin pigmentation.

questions.question_text: Which single-chain peptide hormone acts on the mammary glands to stimulate milk secretion?
questions.explanation: Prolactin stimulates mammary gland development and lactation.

questions.question_text: Which hormone stimulates the hepatic secretion of insulin-like growth factor-1?
questions.explanation: Growth hormone induces the liver to produce IGF-1, mediating its growth-promoting effects.

questions.question_text: The action of which hormone differs in males versus females?
questions.explanation: Luteinizing hormone stimulates testosterone in males and ovulation/estrogen production in females.

questions.question_text: Which hormone stimulates adrenal steroid production?
questions.explanation: ACTH prompts the adrenal cortex to synthesize and secrete cortisol and other steroids.

questions.question_text: This stage of sleep has increased delta activity (approximately 20%–50%).
questions.explanation: Stage 3 sleep features 20%–50% delta waves and is part of NREM deep sleep.

questions.question_text: This stage of sleep has increased delta activity (more than 50%).
questions.explanation: Stage 4 sleep is characterized by over 50% delta wave activity (deepest NREM sleep).

questions.question_text: These two stages of sleep are commonly referred to as slow-wave sleep.
questions.explanation: Stages 3 and 4 are collectively known as slow-wave (delta) sleep.

questions.question_text: In this stage there is marked alpha activity.
questions.explanation: Stage 0 refers to quiet wakefulness with eyes closed and alpha rhythm.

questions.question_text: This stage of sleep is characterized by low-voltage theta activity.
questions.explanation: Stage 1 is light sleep with theta frequency and reduced alpha on EEG.

questions.question_text: This stage of sleep is characterized by occasional sleep spindles and K complexes.
questions.explanation: Stage 2 NREM sleep shows sleep spindles and K complexes on EEG.

questions.question_text: Please select the serotonin–norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor from the options.
questions.explanation: Venlafaxine is a serotonin–norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI).

questions.question_text: Please select the selective noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor from the options.
questions.explanation: Reboxetine is a selective noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor (NARI).

questions.question_text: Please select the noradrenergic and specific serotonergic antidepressant from the options.
questions.explanation: Mirtazapine is a noradrenergic and specific serotonergic antidepressant (NaSSA).

questions.question_text: Please select the nonbenzodiazepine hypnotics from the options.
questions.explanation: Zolpidem and zopiclone are nonbenzodiazepine (“Z”) hypnotics.

questions.question_text: Please select the short-acting benzodiazepine from the options.
questions.explanation: Temazepam is a short-acting benzodiazepine used as a hypnotic.

questions.question_text: Please select the long-acting benzodiazepine from the options.
questions.explanation: Diazepam is a long-acting benzodiazepine.

questions.question_text: Increased volume of distribution is dependent on which factor?
questions.explanation: High lipid solubility increases tissue distribution and thus volume of distribution.

questions.question_text: Which concept relates the mass of a drug in the body to its plasma concentration?
questions.explanation: Volume of distribution (Vd) is the theoretical ratio of drug amount in body to plasma concentration.

questions.question_text: Which refers to a synthetic conjugation reaction between drug and a polar endogenous group?
questions.explanation: Phase II metabolism involves conjugation of drug or metabolite with polar groups (e.g., glucuronidation).

questions.question_text: Which refers to non-synthetic changes in drug structure (oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis)?
questions.explanation: Phase I metabolism involves functionalization reactions (oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis).

questions.question_text: Which effect refers to presystemic metabolism of orally absorbed drugs by the liver?
questions.explanation: The first-pass effect is hepatic metabolism of drug before it reaches systemic circulation.

questions.question_text: At times, abnormalities in mitosis give rise to an abnormal cell line. Which concept is this?
questions.explanation: Mosaicism arises when mitotic errors produce two or more genetically distinct cell lines.

questions.question_text: The phenomenon of earlier onset or increased severity in succeeding generations is called:
questions.explanation: Anticipation describes progressive earlier or more severe expression in later generations.

questions.question_text: Inheriting both homologues of a chromosome pair from the same parent is known as:
questions.explanation: Uniparental disomy occurs when both copies of a chromosome pair are inherited from one parent.

questions.question_text: Which mode of inheritance is strictly maternal?
questions.explanation: Mitochondrial inheritance is exclusively through the maternal line.

questions.question_text: The phenomenon in which an allele is differentially expressed depending on its parental origin is called:
questions.explanation: Genomic imprinting involves parent-of-origin–specific gene expression.

questions.question_text: This form of questioning confirms the validity of a prior judgment or behavior.
questions.explanation: Affirmation validates or confirms clients’ feelings or actions.

questions.question_text: This refers to statements of appreciation rendered during the therapy session.
questions.explanation: Praise consists of positive feedback and acknowledgment to encourage clients.

questions.question_text: This refers to repeating the client’s account by paraphrasing or adding meaning.
questions.explanation: Reflective listening involves paraphrasing and confirming the client’s message.

questions.question_text: This involves providing a logical explanation for an event, situation or outcome.
questions.explanation: Rationalization and reframing offer alternative logical perspectives on a situation.

questions.question_text: This includes offering acknowledging statements as well as validating feelings.
questions.explanation: Expression of interests conveys empathy by acknowledging and validating the client’s emotions.

questions.question_text: This form of psychotherapy works on the premise that symptoms of individual family members are a manifestation of family system functioning.
questions.explanation: Family therapy views individual symptoms as rooted in dysfunctional family interactions.

questions.question_text: This form of psychotherapy has its basis in attachment theory.
questions.explanation:
Interpersonal therapy is based on the attachment theory. The 
objective is to create a therapeutic environment with meaningful therapeutic 
relationship and recognize the client’s underlying attachment needs. It also 
helps to develop an understanding of the client’s communication difficulties and 
attachment style both inside and outside of therapy.

questions.question_text: This form of psychotherapy is particularly helpful for patients with borderline personality disorder.
questions.explanation: Dialectical behavioural therapy (DBT) is specifically designed for borderline personality disorder.

questions.question_text: This form of therapy focuses less on transference interpretation and more on changing specific thinking patterns.
questions.explanation: Cognitive analytic therapy emphasizes procedural sequence modeling and changing maladaptive thinking.

questions.question_text: Contraindications include severe dementia, profound learning disability, delirium or absence of cognitive errors.
questions.explanation: CBT requires cognitive capacity; severe cognitive impairment contraindicates its use.

questions.question_text: The prosencephalon gives rise to the cerebral hemispheres and which three of the following?
questions.explanation: The telencephalon (part of prosencephalon) forms the pallium, corpus striatum and medullary centre (rhinencephalon).

questions.question_text: The epithalamus contains which two of the following?
questions.explanation: The epithalamus includes the habenular and pineal glands.

questions.question_text: The mesencephalon gives rise to which two of the following?
questions.explanation: The mesencephalon develops into the superior and inferior colliculi.

questions.question_text: The rhombencephalon consists of which one of the following?
questions.explanation: The rhombencephalon (hindbrain) gives rise to the pons, cerebellum and medulla.

questions.question_text: Inputs from the hypothalamus and gastrointestinal tract are received by this nerve, which also supplies the lower respiratory and GI tract to the transverse colon.
questions.explanation: The vagus nerve provides parasympathetic innervation to thoracic and most abdominal organs and carries visceral afferents.

questions.question_text: This nerve helps to regulate the lacrimal and salivary glands.
questions.explanation: The facial nerve’s parasympathetic fibers innervate the lacrimal, submandibular and sublingual glands.

questions.question_text: This is the largest of all the cranial nerves.
questions.explanation: The trigeminal nerve (cranial V) is the largest cranial nerve.

questions.question_text: Macroscopic changes including cerebral atrophy, cavum septum pellucidum perforation and thinning of the corpus callosum are observed mainly in which condition?
questions.explanation: Punch-drunk syndrome shows these macroscopic brain changes following repeated head injury.

questions.question_text: In this condition there is minimal cerebral cortex atrophy in rapidly developing cases.
questions.explanation: CJD often shows minimal cortical atrophy early but more pronounced changes in long-term survivors.

questions.question_text: Multiple cerebral infarcts, local or general brain atrophy and ventricular enlargement are typical of which condition?
questions.explanation: Multi-infarct (vascular) dementia shows multiple infarcts, focal atrophy and ventricular enlargement.

questions.question_text: Select three factors in play in the early stages of group therapy according to Yalom.
questions.explanation: Early group factors include instillation of hope, universality and information giving.

questions.question_text: Select four factors in play in the middle stages of group therapy according to Yalom.
questions.explanation: Middle-stage factors include altruism, corrective recapitulation, social learning and interpersonal learning.

questions.question_text: Select two factors in play in the end stage of group therapy according to Yalom.
questions.explanation: End-stage factors include catharsis and existential factors, fostering closure and self-understanding.
